notes.meaning: God told Moses to send twelve men to scout the land of Canaan, choosing one leader from each ancestral tribe. The people had first asked to explore the country, and the Lord permitted it to test their obedience and show them the good land He was giving them. Even though God had already promised them victory, He allowed them to see what lay ahead.

Moses obeyed God's direction and sent the men out from their camp in the Wilderness of Paran. These men were not the chief princes of the tribes, but respected heads and leading men of influence. Selecting trusted leaders ensured that the whole congregation would take their report seriously.

The list of scouts begins with Shammua from Reuben, Shaphat from Simeon, and Caleb from Judah. Each man represented his tribe's share in the future inheritance of the promised country. Caleb would later prove to be an outstanding man of faith who trusted God completely.

The list continues with Igal from Issachar, Hoshea from Ephraim, and Palti from Benjamin. These leaders were picked so that every part of Israel had an eyewitness inside the land. Hoshea, also known as Joshua, was Moses' faithful assistant and future successor.

Next came Gaddiel from Zebulun, Gaddi from the tribe of Manasseh (representing Joseph), and Ammiel from Dan. Having a leader from every tribe made sure the whole nation shared in the mission. Sadly, most of these tribal chiefs later allowed fear to ruin their trust in God.

The list ends with Sethur from Asher, Nahbi from Naphtali, and Geuel from Gad. The priestly tribe of Levi was not included because the Levites had no land territory of their own. This completed the selection of twelve leaders to explore the land for all Israel.

When Moses sent the scouts out, he changed Hoshea's name, which means 'salvation,' to Joshua, which means 'the LORD saves.' This new name was a quiet prophecy that victory would come only through God's power. Joshua stands in Scripture as an Old Testament picture of Jesus, who brings God's people into their true spiritual rest.

Moses instructed the scouts to start by traveling north through the Negev, the dry southern desert, and go up into the central hill country. This was the nearest and most direct way into Canaan, allowing them to enter quietly without drawing immediate attention. From those highlands, they could get a clear view of the surrounding valleys.

Moses told the men to inspect both the land and its people. They needed to find out whether the inhabitants were physically strong and brave or weak and timid, and whether they were few or many in number. This was practical preparation for the battles that lay ahead.

The scouts were also asked to observe the climate and the layout of the towns. Moses wanted to know if the inhabitants lived in open, unprotected camps or in heavily fortified strongholds. Understanding the enemy's defenses was key to Israel's military planning.

Moses asked whether the soil was rich and fertile or poor and barren, and whether forests and orchards grew there. He urged them to be courageous and bring back some of the fruit, since it was late summer when the first grapes ripened. God wanted His people to see proof of the wonderful country He had promised them.

The scouts explored the entire length of the country, starting from the Wilderness of Zin in the south all the way to Rehob near Hamath in the far north. This thorough journey covered about 250 miles and spanned the full borders of the land promised to Abraham. Their trek proved that God had opened every part of the land to their view.

On their way through the southern hills, they visited Hebron, the ancient place where Abraham, Sarah, and Isaac were buried. Three clans of the Anakim lived there, famous for their unusual height and physical power. The writer notes that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt, showing the ancient roots of this sacred site.

In a valley near Hebron, the scouts cut a single cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it on a pole to keep it from being crushed. They also picked fresh pomegranates and figs to show the abundance of the harvests. Because of this enormous bunch of fruit, the Israelites called the place the Valley of Eshcol, which means 'cluster.'

The twelve men returned to the camp after spending forty days scouting the entire country. This gave them plenty of time to study the soil, the fortifications, and the people thoroughly. In Scripture, forty days is often a time of testing, and Israel was now about to face a major test of faith.

The scouts reported back to Moses, Aaron, and the entire assembly of Israel at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Paran. They gave their report publicly and showed everyone the rich fruit they had gathered. The whole camp could see with their own eyes that the land was abundantly fertile.

The scouts began by confirming that Canaan was indeed a land 'flowing with milk and honey,' a traditional saying describing rich pastures and plentiful food. They pointed to the fruit in their hands as proof of God's blessing on the soil. Up to this point, their report agreed entirely with what the Lord had promised.

The report quickly turned negative when ten of the scouts added a fearful 'nevertheless.' They warned that the people were powerful, the cities were enormous and heavily walled, and the towering sons of Anak lived there. By looking at human obstacles instead of God's power, they began planting seeds of panic in the congregation.

The scouts described how different warlike groups held every corner of the country. The fierce Amalekites lived in the southern desert, the Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites guarded the mountains, and the Canaanites controlled the seacoast and Jordan valley. They made it sound as though Israel was completely blocked from entering anywhere.

Seeing the crowd grow agitated and frightened, Caleb stood before Moses and quieted the people. He boldly declared that they should go up at once and conquer the land, insisting they were well able to overcome it. Caleb spoke with courage because his eyes were fixed on God's promise rather than the enemy's strength.

The other ten scouts immediately argued against Caleb, insisting that Israel could not defeat the local armies. They claimed the Canaanites were far stronger than the Israelites in size and numbers. In their fear, they forgot all the miracles God had done in Egypt and looked only at their own human limits.

The fearful scouts spread an evil, discouraging report, claiming that Canaan was a land that 'devours its inhabitants.' This meant either that the territory suffered from endless, bloody warfare or that the climate was deadly to outsiders. They even exaggerated by claiming that every person they met was of gigantic size.

The ten men claimed they had seen the Nephilim, an ancient term used for towering warriors and giants. Beside such huge men, the scouts said they felt as small and powerless as grasshoppers, and they assumed the Canaanites looked down on them with the same contempt. Their fear made the giants look huge and made God look small, which led the whole nation into deep unbelief.
